messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Murray. I am using secr 3.1.0. The Tu plot turns out fine now - thanks for your suggestions.

I thought that calling derived() gave me a better estimate for D. I checked out the help after you said it was a mistake and can see now that I was wrong. I am now getting the same answer that you got: 14 lynx/100 km sq (9-22/ 100 km sq). (Did you round differently for the upper and lower CI? If so, is there a reason you rounded down for the lower and up for the upper?)

I'm still wondering about the buffer warnings that I outlined above. I thought that as long as the buffer warning showed up I should use the fitted model to suggest a new buffer and rerun:
> suggest.buffer(resight17null)
[1] 25966
But the warnings don't let up no matter how big of a buffer I use. I see from your estimate of D that you stopped after fitting the model the first time and did not increase the buffer like I did. That's easier, so I'll run with it, but I would like to know why?

Thanks for helping me with this and for all your work with the secr group.

Darcy

It's a mistake to apply derived(). Admittedly the warning message "use of allsighting here untested" should be stronger - an outright error.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to get my head around the following passage in the polygon detector vignette:

> Although probability and cumulative hazard are mostly interchangeable for point detectors, it’s not so simple for polygon and transect detectors. The integration in equation 1 always uses the hazard form for h(u | x) (secr 3.0.0 and later), and only hazard-based detection functions are allowed (HHN, HHR, HEX, HAN, HCG). The default function is HHN.

I want to fit a model where the PDF of a cue's location is bivariate normal, centred on the activity centre. However, I'm struggling to figure out if this is what the default hazard halfnormal actually gives me, or what the non-hazard halfnormal would give me if secr let me use it.

For example, the hazard halfnormal detection function can have a long shoulder at 1 if lambda0 is large enough. So, if I use the hazard halfnormal here, is it the case that the PDF of a cue's location is not bivariate normal, but rather may have a circular, flat 'plateau' around the activity centre due to this shoulder? If secr did let me fit the non-hazard halfnormal detection function, how would this change the assumed PDF of a cue's location?

Many thanks,

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben
I tried so hard to make that clear in the pdf, but I admit there is still room for the doubt you raise! As I remember/understand, the function h(u|x) should be interpreted directly as the spatial distribution (pdf) of cues - so HHN will give the bivariate normal you ask for. h(u|x) itself is integrated to get the expected number of (detected) cues. You will have read "The detection model is fundamentally different for polygon detectors..." Part of that is that at no point is h(u|x) converted to a probability via e.g. 1-exp(-h(u|x)). If one integrated 1-exp(-h(u|x)) then one would be modelling a different distribution, as you suggest, but 'secr' does not do that. It's somewhat arbitrary that 'secr' uses HHN rather than HN etc. for polygon detectors (I feel comfortable integrating hazards or probability densities, but not probabilities).
Hope this gives you some confidence...
Murray

Hi again

Were you really needing to use detectfn = 'HR'? That is the source of the trouble.
1. When you simulate data with detectfn='HR' but do not specify the third parameter z, sim.capthist (called by run.scenarios) defaults to z = 1. With your other settings that results in a very fat tail, truncated at the mask buffer radius.
2. The fat tail results in very large numbers of detections - probably more than you really expect.
3. As you do not specify the detectfn to fit, secr.fit (again called by run.scenarios) defaults to HN. However the "true" HR value of sigma (30 m) is a terrible starting value for the HN sigma needed to model the flat, wide detections from the HR model with z=1, and the likelihood computation bombs.

I suggest keeping things simple (detectfn='HN' throughout). The alternative is to grapple with the various issues (specifying detectfn in fit.args etc.). Using HR (or HHR) is always risky.

The other warning message can probably be ignored - I'll clean it up in the next release.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
I often use extractfn = identity and manipulate the resulting list of lists of secr fitted models, but this takes a lot of space when nrepl is large and can test your R skills. More directly, why not use the coef function?

## a simple example
scen1 <- make.scenarios(D = c(5,10), sigma = 25, g0 = 0.2, noccasions =
                            c(5,10))
traps1 <- make.grid()   ## default 6 x 6 trap grid
tmp1 <- run.scenarios(nrepl = 2, trapset = traps1, scenarios = scen1,
                      fit.args = list(model=g0~b), fit = TRUE, extractfn = coef)
## selecting one coefficient (i.e. one row in coef table)
summary(tmp1, parameter = 'g0.bTRUE')

Murray

I don't know MARK that well, but I expect the answer is Yes

>
> Is it ever ok to use the hazard rate detection function? When I use AIC to compare models with differnt detection functions, the models with hazard rate or exponential detection functions always have the smallest AIC values. In most of the stuff I have read, using hazard rate is discouraged unless there is some kind of boundary. The population I am studying is on an island. Is it therefore ok to use the hazard rate detection function? I only ask because the density estimates are considerably different depending on which detection function is used.

The main problem with the hazard-rate function, andalso  the reason it may fit better than say halfnormal, is its long tail, which accommodates occasional long movements. A long tail means that very distant animals have a chance to get caught and the population at risk of detection is enormous. On an island there will be a natural boundary rather than an arbitrary cutoff, so this is less of a worry. The exponential function serves nearly the same purpose but is better behaved in the tail. If the different detection functions result in very different estimates I would be careful - those long movements may be having far too much influence.

> Lastly, I would like to calculate population change (lambda= Dt+1/Dt) and the associated standard error (SE(lambdai) =  ).
>
>
>  Is there any way that I can extract the variance estimate for density from a fitted model so that I can calculate SE(lambdai)?
>
>

I don't quite get the question. 'secr' reports SE for density. If you are interested in multiplicative population change between sessions then the beta coefficient D.Session of a model with D ~ Session (not capital S) is log(lambda) (assuming the default log link for density). So lambda-hat = exp(beta-hat) and SE(lambda-hat) = exp(beta-hat) * sqrt(exp(sebeta-hat^2)-1) (the standard delta approximation used in 'secr'). For the ovenbird example in 'secr'
beta <- coef(ovenbird.model.D)['D.Session', 'beta']
sebeta <- coef(ovenbird.model.D)['D.Session', 'SE.beta']
exp(beta)
[1] 0.9381417
exp(beta) * sqrt(exp(sebeta^2)-1)
[1] 0.06589315
# 95% CI by backtransforming limits on log scale
exp(coef(ovenbird.model.D)['D.Session', c('lcl','ucl')])
                lcl     ucl
D.Session 0.8176272 1.07642

Murray

> >  Is there any way that I can extract the variance estimate for density from a fitted model so that I can calculate SE(lambdai)?

>
> I don't quite get the question. 'secr' reports SE for density. If you are interested in multiplicative population change between sessions then the beta coefficient D.Session of a model with D ~ Session (not capital S) is log(lambda) (assuming the default log link for density). So lambda-hat = exp(beta-hat) and SE(lambda-hat) = exp(beta-hat) * sqrt(exp(sebeta-hat^2)-1) (the standard delta approximation used in 'secr'). For the ovenbird example in 'secr'
> beta <- coef(ovenbird.model.D)['D.Session', 'beta']
> sebeta <- coef(ovenbird.model.D)['D.Session', 'SE.beta']
> exp(beta)
> [1] 0.9381417
> exp(beta) * sqrt(exp(sebeta^2)-1)
> [1] 0.06589315
> # 95% CI by backtransforming limits on log scale
> exp(coef(ovenbird.model.D)['D.Session', c('lcl','ucl')])
>                 lcl     ucl
> D.Session 0.8176272 1.07642
>

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to use half-normal estimates of sigma to calculate 95% home ranges.
It seems the following formula: (95HR = 2.45^2 * Pi * sigma^2 ; roughly 19 * sigma^2) was mentioned during an SECR workshop in Montpellier (but I don't have any reference to use it). The HR estimates I get using this formula are slightly big but reasonable.

While searching for previous conversations on the subject, I found this question sent to the secrgroup a little bit more than a year ago:

It was highlighted that the sigma should not be directly compared between half-normal and negative exponential detection functions. Is there a simple way to estimate a 'home range radius' and a '95% home range area' from a negative exponential sigma? For the half-normal sigma I have generally used these formula (based on Ringler et al. 2014 and Noss et al. 2012):
HR_radius<-(qchisq(0.95,2)^0.5)*(sigma)
HR95_area<-(pi*(3.36*sigma)^2)/10000

Looking at the Ringler et al. 2014 paper (attached), the underlying idea behind the formula seems to be the same (5% chi-squared test statistic), but the factor jumped from 19 to 35, which in my case will lead to HR estimates unreasonably big.

My question is: which formula should I use to estimate 95% Home Range from sigma and which reference must I provide?

Thanks very much
Kind regards,

Elsa

Hi
Check the help for circular.r in 'secr'. The bivariate-normal multiplier is indeed around 19 (it also depends on whether you believe the hazard or the probability has a bivariate normal distribution). I think one of Beth Gardner's papers is a peer-reviewed source for SECR, and there are many others going back to Calhoun & Casby and Jennrich & Turner. I can't make sense of Ringler et al. They use a hazard-rate detection function for which the multiplier depends strongly on z, yet, as far as I can see on a quick browse, they do not acknowledge this or report their z-hat.

Whatever you do - remember this is really rough and depends on an implausible model for animal behaviour, so agreement with telemetry data is not expected.
Murray
